title: Continuous Diffusion Scales Competitively with Discrete Diffusion for Language

paper.title: Continuous Diffusion Scales Competitively with Discrete Diffusion for Language
paper.abstract: Abstract While diffusion has drawn considerable recent attention from the language modeling community, continuous diffusion has appeared less scalable than discrete approaches. To challenge this belief we revisit Plaid, a likelihood-based continuous diffusion language model (DLM), and construct RePlaid by aligning the architecture of Plaid with modern discrete DLMs. In this unified setting, we establish the first scaling law for continuous DLMs that rivals discrete DLMs: RePlaid exhibits a compute gap of only 20 × 20\times compared to autoregressive models, outperforms Duo while using fewer parameters, and outperforms MDLM in the over-trained regime. We benchmark RePlaid against recent continuous DLMs: on OpenWebText, RePlaid achieves a new state-of-the-art PPL bound of 22.1 22.1 among continuous DLMs and superior generation quality. These results suggest that continuous diffusion, when trained via likelihood, is a highly competitive and scalable alternative to discrete DLMs. Moreover, we offer theoretical insights to understand the advantage of likelihood-based training. We show that optimizing the noise schedule to minimize the ELBO’s variance naturally yields linear cross-entropy (information loss) over time. This evenly distributes denoising difficulty without any case-specific time reparameterization. In addition, we find that optimizing embeddings via likelihood creates structured geometries and drives the most significant likelihood gain.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Discrete diffusion language models (DLMs) show significant promise, increasingly rivaling the performance and scalability of autoregressive (AR) models across various benchmarks [ 36 , 60 ] . Despite these successes, continuous diffusion remains a compelling alternative due to its inherent potential for controllability and acceleration. The smooth geometry of a continuous latent space enables structured editing [ 35 , 11 ] and allows for the application of efficient ODE-based solvers [ 71 , 32 ] , facilitating distillation of complex sampling trajectories into high-fidelity, single-step generators [ 52 , 58 ] . Unlike discrete diffusion, which often suffers from severe quality degradation under limited sampling budgets, continuous diffusion offers a principled path toward efficient text generation by enabling superior trade-offs between computational cost and sample quality [ 27 , 26 ] . While continuous DLMs present unique advantages, previous work finds a significant training scalability gap compared to discrete DLMs. Previous studies show empirical evidence that continuous diffusion underperforms discrete diffusion and AR models when evaluated at equivalent training FLOPs and parameter counts [ 2 , 17 ] ; the original Plaid study reported a significant 64 × 64\times compute overhead compared to autoregressive models to achieve matching likelihood [ 17 ] . This figure is frequently cited as evidence of the poor scalability of continuous DLMs. By revisiting this principled likelihood-based paradigm, we aim to determine whether this performance gap is an inherent limitation of continuous diffusion or a consequence of incompatible scaling analyses. To address this question, we introduce RePlaid , a revised version of Plaid featuring a transformer architecture carefully aligned with modern discrete DLM practices. While the original 64 × 64\times gap suggested continuous diffusion was impractical at scale, those findings were obtained under a different setup from the protocols used to establish current discrete diffusion scaling laws. By adopting the exact protocol from Sahoo et al. [50] —including the same dataset, optimization hyperparameters, and compute budget—we perform the first unified scaling comparison between continuous and discrete DLMs. Crucially, in this controlled environment, the performance gap narrows to 20 × 20\times for RePlaid versus AR, placing continuous diffusion on par with discrete diffusion and challenging the narrative of its inherent unscalability. Furthermore, we find that RePlaid achieves consistent improvements in generation quality over other recent continuous models like FLM [ 28 ] and LangFlow [ 9 ] . In contrast to other recent work, RePlaid’s training objective (like Plaid) is explicitly derived from a likelihood bound (ELBO) , providing a theoretically grounded framework for training that heuristic cross-entropy or flow-matching methods lack. We attribute the success of RePlaid to two primary factors: ( i ) (i) optimizing the noise schedule via ELBO variance naturally recovers a near-linear cross-entropy schedule that evenly distributes denoising difficulty without heuristic reparameterization, and ( i ​ i ) (ii) ELBO-based embedding optimization inherently regularizes the latent geometry to improve likelihood, creating a structured, low-entropy space that prevents potential token dispersion in cross-entropy-based training. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • RePlaid & Benchmarking: We introduce RePlaid, a modernized likelihood-based DLM achieving a state-of-the-art 22.1 22.1 perplexity among existing continuous DLMs on OpenWebText. • Unified Scaling Analysis: We present the first unified scaling law comparison between continuous and discrete DLMs, showing that continuous models scale on par with discrete counterparts when properly aligned. • Theoretical Insights: We show that the ELBO objective: ( i ) (i) naturally recovers a linear cross-entropy noise schedule, eliminating heuristic time reparameterizations, and ( i ​ i ) (ii) inherently regularizes embedding geometry for likelihood improvement and prevents token dispersion.

sections.heading: Beyond VDMs.
sections.text: On top of VDMs, Plaid adds two features besides the categorical reparameterization 𝐞 θ = 𝐱 θ ​ 𝐄 {\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}={\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}{\mathbf{E}} . First, it uses a learnable encoding via the embedding matrix 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} . Second, it adds self-conditioning [ 8 ] : during training, for 25 % 25\% of each batch the denoiser performs an initial gradient-free forward pass to estimate the clean data, which is fed back as an additional conditioning input for the actual prediction; at validation and sampling time, self-conditioning is enabled for all examples.

sections.heading: Cheaper embedding operations.
sections.text: Although largely overlooked in the current literature, Plaid offers substantially cheaper embedding operations compared to DLMs that inject Gaussian noise into high-dimensional (e.g., one-hot [ 28 , 47 , 44 ] ) embeddings. For example, projecting V V -dimensional one-hot embeddings to the transformer hidden size h h requires an FP32 matrix multiplication of [ L , V ] × [ V , h ] [L,V]\times[V,h] . Plaid reduces this to [ L , d e ] × [ d e , h ] [L,d_{e}]\times[d_{e},h] plus categorical reparameterization [ L , V ] × [ V , d e ] [L,V]\times[V,d_{e}] at the output, which requires ≈ 50 × \approx 50\times fewer FLOPs when V ≈ 50 V\approx 50 K (e.g., GPT-2 [ 46 ] ), h = 768 h=768 , and d e = 16 d_{e}=16 .

sections.heading: 3 Revisiting Scaling Laws of Continuous DLMs
sections.text: In this section, we introduce RePlaid: a revised version of Plaid using a transformer architecture that is carefully aligned with modern discrete DLMs. This alignment allows us to benchmark RePlaid against discrete DLMs using the scaling law protocol from Sahoo et al. [50] . We find that RePlaid’s scaling is on par with discrete diffusion: to achieve the same validation loss as AR, RePlaid requires 20 × 20\times compute with self-conditioning, and 27 × 27\times compute without it. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unified scaling comparison between continuous and discrete DLMs.

sections.heading: 3.1 RePlaid: Aligning Plaid with Modern Discrete DLM Architecture
sections.text: In Sahoo et al. [50] , MDLM and Duo employ a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [ 42 ] equipped with bidirectional attention, RoPE [ 62 ] , and AdaLN-Zero [ 42 ] . The autoregressive (AR) baseline utilizes an identical architecture, differing only in its use of causal attention. For RePlaid, we retain all foundational algorithmic components of Plaid ( Sec. 2 ) while fully aligning its transformer architecture to match the one used by MDLM and Duo. Specifically, this alignment incorporates LayerNorm, MLP biases, GELU(tanh) activations, and AdaLN-Zero modulation with learnable gating for residual connections. In addition, the original Plaid computes its final logit head in FP32 due to its interaction with output prior logits ( Sec. 2 ). We remove this substantial numerical confounder for fair comparison. See App. J for a detailed pre- and post-alignment comparison on architecture and numerical precision.

sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: We utilize the large-scale, deduplicated SlimPajama dataset [ 56 ] , which provides a sufficiently rich distribution to avoid data repetition during training. We use the Llama-2 tokenizer [ 63 ] ( V = 32,001 V=32{,}001 with a special mask token), a batch size of 256 256 , and a sequence length of 2048 2048 tokens.

sections.heading: Optimization.
sections.text: AR, MDLM, and Duo use AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule decaying from 2 ​ e − 4 2{\mathrm{e}}{-}4 to 2 ​ e − 5 2{\mathrm{e}}{-}5 , alongside β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}{=}0.9 and β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}{=}0.95 and 1 % 1\% learning rate warmup (minimum 100 100 steps). Parameters are regularized with a weight decay of 0.1 0.1 without dropout. RePlaid applies this identical configuration, with minor adjustments to accommodate its learnable noise schedule and its length-normalized, low-dimensional ( d e = 16 d_{e}=16 ) embeddings ( Tab. 7 ), following Plaid. For reference, optimizing the 231 231 M MDLM for 1 ​ e ​ 20 1{\mathrm{e}}20 FLOPs requires about 32 32 hours on 8 8 NVIDIA GB200s.

sections.text: We measure non-embedding FLOPs using calflops [ 68 ] . Self-conditioning of 25 % 25\% increases the non-embedding FLOPs by ≈ 8.3 % \approx 8.3\% , which we offset by reducing training steps.

sections.heading: Competitive loss scaling.
sections.text: Fig. 2(a) shows that RePlaid scales competitively with discrete DLMs. The compute-optimal loss for RePlaid (s.c.) exhibits power-law scaling, decreasing at a rate comparable to AR, MDLM, and Duo. The ≈ 20 × \approx 20\times compute gap of RePlaid (s.c.) outperforms Duo ( ≈ 22 × \approx 22\times ) and approaches MDLM ( ≈ 14 × \approx 14\times ). RePlaid (no s.c.) exhibits a gap of ≈ 27 × \approx 27\times , approaching Duo.

sections.heading: Strong parameter efficiency.
sections.text: RePlaid also demonstrates significant parameter efficiency. To reach its compute-optimal frontier, RePlaid requires ≈ 3.4 × \approx 3.4\times fewer parameters than the AR baseline ( Fig. 2(b) ). Crucially, RePlaid (s.c.) uses ≈ 1.8 × \approx 1.8\times fewer parameters than MDLM and Duo ( Fig. 2(b) ), achieving this size reduction while outperforming Duo’s compute-optimal loss ( Fig. 2(a) ).

sections.heading: Outperforming MDLM at over-training.
sections.text: Obtaining high-quality small models through over-training is critical for heavy inference [ 53 ] . RePlaid (s.c.) offers distinct advantages when training past compute-optimal budgets to minimize inference costs. A crossover occurs in this over-trained regime ( Fig. 1 , below green line), where RePlaid (s.c.) predictably achieves a lower loss than MDLM. More precisely, for a given model size, a RePlaid (s.c.) trained for ≈ 3.1 × \approx 3.1\times its optimal compute matches the loss of an MDLM trained for ≈ 6.9 × \approx 6.9\times its optimal compute ( Fig. 2(b) , green line).

sections.heading: 4 Benchmarking RePlaid for Diffusion Language Models
sections.text: The 0.1 0.1 B regime is the standard testbed for DLMs where the recent wave of continuous DLMs [ 28 , 9 , 47 , 44 ] is exclusively benchmarked. Having shown in Sec. 3 that RePlaid scales on par with discrete DLMs, we now compare at this canonical scale against the strongest discrete (MDLM [ 48 ] , Duo [ 49 ] ) and continuous (FLM [ 28 ] , LangFlow [ 9 ] ) DLMs along likelihood ( Sec. 4.1 ) and sample quality ( Sec. 4.2 ). Both are necessary: FLM does not propose a likelihood bound; in addition, recent works [ 49 , 50 ] have shown that better likelihood may not always lead to better sample quality.

sections.heading: Unified setup.
sections.text: AR, MDLM, Duo, FLM, LangFlow, and RePlaid use the same transformer architecture used in Sec. 3 . During sampling, we vary the number of diffusion discretization steps T T (not including the final argmax \argmax ) to control NFEs. For MDLM, Duo, FLM, and LangFlow, we use their official, publicly available 1M checkpoints. We measure Generative perplexity (GenPPL) [ 14 ] via GPT-2 Large [ 46 ] , MAUVE [ 43 ] via ModernBERT-Large [ 67 ] for sample quality, and average unigram entropy for diversity [ 72 ] . GenPPL is the standard metric used in prior work [ 48 , 49 , 28 , 44 , 9 ] . RePlaid (s.c.) struggles at low sampling steps (as with LangFlow) but further improves upon RePlaid (no s.c.) for T ≥ 64 T\geq 64 , outperforming discrete DLMs and other continuous DLMs with self-conditioning at high sampling steps. sections.heading: 5 Theoretical Insights
sections.text: Having shown that RePlaid attains the best PPL bound and sample quality among continuous DLMs on OpenWebText, we now ask why, given that its training objective is a plain VDM NELBO with neither cross-entropy (CE) nor hand-engineered time reparameterization [ 14 , 28 , 44 , 47 , 9 ] . We argue that the answer is in the NELBO itself: it is a true upper bound on the negative log-likelihood while the alternatives are not, and thus the rest of this section traces two consequences of optimizing this bound. ( i ) (i) Adding an extra CE term to the NELBO provides a separative force on the learned embeddings 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} , which disrupts the low-rank embedding structure and hurts the PPL; ( i ​ i ) (ii) Making the noise schedule a learnable part of the NELBO and training it to minimize Monte-Carlo variance automatically yields a constant per-timestep diffusion loss and a near-linear per-timestep CE —the time-uniformity property recent CE-based methods engineer with manually-designed time reparameterization.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.text: We present the first unified scaling law comparison between continuous and discrete DLMs, showing that continuous models scale on par with discrete counterparts when properly aligned in architecture and experimental setting. We introduce RePlaid, a modernized likelihood-based continuous DLM achieving a state-of-the-art 22.1 22.1 perplexity among continuous DLMs on OpenWebText and even rivaling discrete DLMs in terms of both likelihood and sample quality. We show that the ELBO objective: ( i ) (i) naturally recovers near-linear cross-entropy over time, eliminating heuristic time reparameterizations, and ( i ​ i ) (ii) inherently regularizes embedding geometry for likelihood improvement and prevents potential token dispersion in cross-entropy-based training. While our scaling law study provides a rigorous comparison following prior work on scaling discrete DLMs [ 38 , 50 ] , we acknowledge that a 20 × 20\times compute gap remains between RePlaid and AR models to achieve matching likelihood. Investigating whether these scaling trends persist in the multi-billion-parameter regime where modern LLMs operate is a critical next step. Furthermore, our analysis identifies learnable token embeddings as the primary driver of RePlaid’s perplexity gains; extending this framework with richer contextual encoders [ 37 ] that condition on the full sequence represents a promising path forward. Finally, the continuous nature of RePlaid opens unique avenues for efficiency research unavailable to discrete diffusion, most notably the distillation of sampling trajectories via the PFODE and the exploration of latent-space inference-time scaling.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Works
sections.text: This appendix surveys diffusion-based approaches to language generation. We do not attempt to review the dominant autoregressive paradigm [ 65 , 46 ] , which serves as the reference baseline in our scaling-law comparisons ( Sec. 3 ). Diffusion-based language models split into two families: discrete diffusion, which defines a Markov forward process directly on tokens, and continuous diffusion, which lifts tokens into a continuous space and runs a Gaussian (or Riemannian) diffusion there.

sections.heading: A.1 Discrete diffusion language models
sections.text: Discrete diffusion was introduced by D3PM [ 2 ] , which defined absorbing-state and uniform-noise transition kernels over token sequences and was lifted to continuous-time Markov chains shortly after [ 5 ] . Subsequent work refined the parameterization: SEDD [ 30 ] and concrete score matching [ 34 ] replaced the categorical denoising objective with a score-matching surrogate, while MDLM [ 48 ] , MD4 [ 55 ] and RADD [ 41 ] concurrently and independently identified that the absorbing-state model collapses to a clean per-position cross-entropy objective once the mask token is treated correctly. Block Diffusion [ 1 ] and Eso-LMs [ 51 ] interpolate between masked diffusion and autoregressive decoding to obtain unified families. In parallel, discrete flow matching [ 15 ] and generative flows on discrete state spaces [ 6 ] cast the discrete forward process in a flow-matching framework, and LLaDA [ 39 ] and Dream [ 70 ] scale masked diffusion to 7–8B parameters. Most relevant to our methodology, Nie et al. [38] and Sahoo et al. [50] provide the IsoFLOP scaling-law protocol that we adopt to benchmark continuous diffusion against its discrete counterparts on equal footing.

sections.heading: A.2 Continuous diffusion language models
sections.text: Continuous diffusion language modeling lifts a Gaussian forward process onto a continuous representation of tokens, and falls roughly into three camps. The first and most studied embeds tokens into ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} and diffuses the embeddings: Diffusion-LM [ 29 ] and SSD-LM [ 19 ] introduced the recipe with controllable generation in mind; CDCD [ 14 ] added a learned categorical-conditional schedule; DiffusionBERT [ 20 ] and self-conditioned embedding diffusion [ 61 ] explored hybrid masked/continuous training; latent diffusion language models [ 31 ] push the diffusion into a frozen pretrained latent space; and analog bits [ 8 ] encode tokens as binary vectors and diffuse them in ℝ \mathbb{R} . Plaid [ 17 ] , on which RePlaid is directly based, combined low-dimensional sphere-normalized embeddings, a softmax-categorical denoiser and a learned monotone noise schedule. Concurrent work continues this thread: FLM [ 28 ] recasts the embedding-space diffusion as a flow-map model targeting one-step continuous denoising, and Discrete Flow Maps (DFM) [ 44 ] and Categorical Flow Maps (CFM) [ 47 ] are concurrent works that extend the flow-map machinery further. Both FLM and DFM uses fixed one-hot embeddings and cross-entropy loss. LangFlow [ 9 ] swaps the three-term NELBO in Plaid for a pure cross-entropy objective justified via a Bregman flow-matching identity, and uses learnable embeddings as in Plaid. A second camp parameterizes the diffusion on the simplex or its statistical manifold rather than in embedding space: categorical flow matching on statistical manifolds [ 10 ] , Fisher flow matching [ 13 ] and RDLM [ 25 ] construct flows respecting the Fisher–Rao geometry of categorical distributions. A third dequantization-based camp lifts categorical samples to continuous variables via argmax flows [ 23 ] or Dirichlet noise [ 3 ] ; Duo [ 49 ] also belongs here, observing that uniform-state discrete diffusion arises as the argmax projection of an underlying Gaussian diffusion and exploiting this duality to import continuous-diffusion training tricks back into the discrete model. RePlaid revisits the embedding-space camp—specifically Plaid—under the IsoFLOP scaling protocol of Nie et al. [38] , Sahoo et al. [50] , isolating what fraction of Plaid’s reported compute gap stems from the method itself versus from the evaluation setup.

[9] and our pipeline resolve 𝐱 sc {\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}} at every solver step from a single bootstrap forward pass with 𝐱 sc ← 𝟎 {\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}\leftarrow{\mathbf{0}} : 𝐱 sc ​ ( 𝐳 ~ , γ ) := 𝐱 θ ​ ( 𝐳 ~ , γ , 𝟎 ) ​ 𝐄 , {\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},\gamma):={\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},\gamma,{\mathbf{0}}){\mathbf{E}}, making 𝐱 sc {\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}} a deterministic function of the current state. sections.heading: Why dropping the chain-rule term inflates the estimate?
sections.text: The PFODE drift 𝐯 ~ θ \tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta} contains a denoising contribution that contracts the trajectory toward the network’s predicted clean embedding 𝐱 ^ θ ​ ( 𝐳 ~ , γ , 𝐱 sc ) ​ 𝐄 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},\gamma,{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}){\mathbf{E}} ; with self-conditioning enabled, the bootstrap 𝐱 sc ​ ( 𝐳 ~ , γ ) {\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},\gamma) co-moves with 𝐳 ~ \tilde{\mathbf{z}} in the high-SNR regime where the prediction is most informative, so the closed-loop velocity actually integrated by the solver is less sensitive to perturbations of 𝐳 ~ \tilde{\mathbf{z}} than the open-loop velocity 𝐯 ~ θ ​ ( ⋅ , γ , 𝐱 sc ⋆ ) \tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}(\cdot,\gamma,{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}^{\star}) that the cached Hutchinson trace estimator probes. Equivalently, since ∂ 𝐱 sc 𝐯 ~ θ ∝ − α γ ∂ 𝐱 sc 𝐱 ^ θ 𝐄 \partial_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}}\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}\propto-\alpha_{\gamma}\,\partial_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}\,{\mathbf{E}} , the missing chain-rule trace tr ⁡ ( ∂ 𝐱 sc 𝐯 ~ θ ⋅ ∂ 𝐳 𝐱 sc ) \operatorname{tr}(\partial_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}}\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}\cdot\partial_{\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}}) is typically negative for a self-conditioning denoiser whose two input pathways agree on the same predicted token. Dropping a negative summand overestimates the integrated divergence ∫ 0 1 ∇ ⋅ 𝐯 θ ​ 𝑑 t \int_{0}^{1}\nabla\cdot{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}\,{\mathrm{d}}t , which via the Liouville closure 22 inflates log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) \log p_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}) and the log-weight log ⁡ w ( k ) \log w^{(k)} , deflating the reported PPL. The bias grows with ∂ 𝐳 𝐱 sc \partial_{\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{sc}} and is therefore largest in the high-SNR regime where the bootstrap is most accurate.

sections.text: We evaluate the estimator on RePlaid and on the publicly released LangFlow checkpoint 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/Continuous-Rivals-Discrete/langflow-owt as an external sanity check, using the chain-rule-corrected drift of Sec. E.2 . Unless stated otherwise, all numbers are computed on a fixed 1024 1024 -sequence subset of the OpenWebText-valid split (GPT2 tokenizer, sequence length 1024 1024 ). The γ \gamma -space PFODE of Lem. 2 is integrated with a 128 128 -step Heun2 solver ( heun2-128 ). The divergence term is estimated by Hutchinson’s estimator with n hutch = 1 n_{\mathrm{hutch}}=1 Rademacher random vector per call. The Jacobian-vector product is approximated by central finite differences with step size h = 0.001 h=0.001 rather than forward-mode automatic differentiation ( torch.func.jvp ), since the latter currently forces PyTorch’s much slower math SDPA backend. The same sequences and self-conditioning protocol are used for both the K K -IWAE and the matched VDM NELBO baseline.

sections.heading: Appendix O Sampling with Temperature
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 4.2 in the main paper] By default, all of our headline sampling comparisons are sampled at temperature τ = 1 \tau=1 , i.e., no temperature sampling. Pynadath et al. [45] discussed the necessity of performing temperature sweeps and report GenPPL-entropy frontiers at each sampling budget T T , as GenPPL can be made artificially low (good) by collapsing entropy. We tackle this problem by reporting MAUVE [ 43 ] , a metric designed to capture both quality and diversity. Empirically, MAUVE assigns low scores to methods that achieve low GenPPL but low entropy (e.g., see FLM in Fig. 3 ). To complement the τ = 1 \tau=1 comparison, we additionally sweep τ \tau for each method to trace out its GenPPL–entropy Pareto frontier, following CANDI [ 45 ] . We control τ \tau by scaling the logits of 𝐱 θ {\mathbf{x}}_{\theta} (as done in CANDI), rather than the score-temperature mechanism used in the original Plaid [ 14 , 17 ] ; we found score temperature to perform substantially worse at low NFE but slightly better at high NFE in the low-entropy regime. The final argmax \argmax readout at t = 0 t=0 is unaffected by τ \tau . sections.heading: Appendix P Computing Dominant POS Tags per GPT-2 Subword
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 5.1 in the main paper] To analyze embedding geometry conditioned on syntactic role, we precompute a dominant Universal POS tag for each GPT-2 subword token over a reference corpus. The challenge is that GPT-2 BPE splits words into subwords (e.g., running → \rightarrow ␣run , ning ), whereas POS tags are defined on whole words. We resolve this by aligning subwords to spaCy [ 22 ] word spans via character offsets.

sections.heading: P.1 Pipeline
sections.text: Given a corpus of token-id rows of length L = 1024 L=1024 , we proceed as follows: 1. Decode. Convert each row of token ids back to text using the GPT-2 tokenizer. 2. Tag. Run spaCy’s POS tagger on the decoded text to obtain word-level tags and their character offsets. 3. Re-encode. Re-tokenize the decoded text with the fast GPT-2 tokenizer to recover (token_id, char_span) pairs for each subword. We use the re-encoded ids rather than the original ids because chunk boundaries in the dataset may truncate multi-byte UTF-8 sequences; re-encoding guarantees that subword spans align with the actual text spaCy saw. 4. Align. For each subword, inherit the POS tag of the spaCy word with which its character span maximally overlaps. 5. Tally. Accumulate a count matrix C ∈ ℤ V × P C\in\mathbb{Z}^{V\times P} where V V is the vocabulary size and P = 18 P{=}18 tags (17 UPOS tags plus a Space bucket). The dominant tag for token v v is argmax p C v , p \argmax_{p}C_{v,p} .

Affiliation: NVIDIA Email: mmardani@nvidia.com John Thickstun † † footnotemark: Affiliation: Cornell Email: jthickstun@cornell.edu Abstract While diffusion has drawn considerable recent attention from the language modeling community, continuous diffusion has appeared less scalable than discrete approaches. To challenge this belief we revisit Plaid, a likelihood-based continuous diffusion language model (DLM), and construct RePlaid by aligning the architecture of Plaid with modern discrete DLMs. In this unified setting, we establish the first scaling law for continuous DLMs that rivals discrete DLMs: RePlaid exhibits a compute gap of only 20 × 20\times compared to autoregressive models, outperforms Duo while using fewer parameters, and outperforms MDLM in the over-trained regime. We benchmark RePlaid against recent continuous DLMs: on OpenWebText, RePlaid achieves a new state-of-the-art PPL bound of 22.1 22.1 among continuous DLMs and superior generation quality. These results suggest that continuous diffusion, when trained via likelihood, is a highly competitive and scalable alternative to discrete DLMs. Moreover, we offer theoretical insights to understand the advantage of likelihood-based training. We show that optimizing the noise schedule to minimize the ELBO’s variance naturally yields linear cross-entropy (information loss) over time. This evenly distributes denoising difficulty without any case-specific time reparameterization. In addition, we find that optimizing embeddings via likelihood creates structured geometries and drives the most significant likelihood gain. 1 Introduction Discrete diffusion language models (DLMs) show significant promise, increasingly rivaling the performance and scalability of autoregressive (AR) models across various benchmarks [ 36 , 60 ] . Despite these successes, continuous diffusion remains a compelling alternative due to its inherent potential for controllability and acceleration. The smooth geometry of a continuous latent space enables structured editing [ 35 , 11 ] and allows for the application of efficient ODE-based solvers [ 71 , 32 ] , facilitating distillation of complex sampling trajectories into high-fidelity, single-step generators [ 52 , 58 ] . Unlike discrete diffusion, which often suffers from severe quality degradation under limited sampling budgets, continuous diffusion offers a principled path toward efficient text generation by enabling superior trade-offs between computational cost and sample quality [ 27 , 26 ] . While continuous DLMs present unique advantages, previous work finds a significant training scalability gap compared to discrete DLMs. Previous studies show empirical evidence that continuous diffusion underperforms discrete diffusion and AR models when evaluated at equivalent training FLOPs and parameter counts [ 2 , 17 ] ; the original Plaid study reported a significant 64 × 64\times compute overhead compared to autoregressive models to achieve matching likelihood [ 17 ] . This figure is frequently cited as evidence of the poor scalability of continuous DLMs. By revisiting this principled likelihood-based paradigm, we aim to determine whether this performance gap is an inherent limitation of continuous diffusion or a consequence of incompatible scaling analyses. To address this question, we introduce RePlaid , a revised version of Plaid featuring a transformer architecture carefully aligned with modern discrete DLM practices. While the original 64 × 64\times gap suggested continuous diffusion was impractical at scale, those findings were obtained under a different setup from the protocols used to establish current discrete diffusion scaling laws. By adopting the exact protocol from Sahoo et al. [50] —including the same dataset, optimization hyperparameters, and compute budget—we perform the first unified scaling comparison between continuous and discrete DLMs. Crucially, in this controlled environment, the performance gap narrows to 20 × 20\times for RePlaid versus AR, placing continuous diffusion on par with discrete diffusion and challenging the narrative of its inherent unscalability. Furthermore, we find that RePlaid achieves consistent improvements in generation quality over other recent continuous models like FLM [ 28 ] and LangFlow [ 9 ] . In contrast to other recent work, RePlaid’s training objective (like Plaid) is explicitly derived from a likelihood bound (ELBO) , providing a theoretically grounded framework for training that heuristic cross-entropy or flow-matching methods lack. We attribute the success of RePlaid to two primary factors: ( i ) (i) optimizing the noise schedule via ELBO variance naturally recovers a near-linear cross-entropy schedule that evenly distributes denoising difficulty without heuristic reparameterization, and ( i ​ i ) (ii) ELBO-based embedding optimization inherently regularizes the latent geometry to improve likelihood, creating a structured, low-entropy space that prevents potential token dispersion in cross-entropy-based training. [50] , MDLM and Duo employ a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [ 42 ] equipped with bidirectional attention, RoPE [ 62 ] , and AdaLN-Zero [ 42 ] . We argue that the answer is in the NELBO itself: it is a true upper bound on the negative log-likelihood while the alternatives are not, and thus the rest of this section traces two consequences of optimizing this bound.
